title: Dry-run code
objective: Predict what a short function returns by tracking its variables line by line, before running it.

sources.title: Myers, Sandler and Badgett, The Art of Software Testing, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2011): desk checking, reading code by hand to find errors

simplifies: The trace shows one variable changing at a time. Real code often has several changing at once; the habit is the same: write each value down as the line runs, never guess ahead.

quiz.prompt: largest([5, 5, 2]) runs. How many times does line 5 (best = nums[i]) run?

options.explanation: Right. best starts at 5; the second 5 is not greater than 5 (line 4 uses >), and 2 is smaller, so line 5 never runs.
No. That would need a number strictly greater than the current best. 5 > 5 is false.
No. Line 5 only runs when nums[i] is greater than best, and neither 5 nor 2 is greater than 5.

quiz.prompt: What would largest([]) do with this code?

options.explanation: No. Nothing in the code returns 0; it never gets that far.

options.text: Fail on line 2, because nums[0] doesn't exist
options.explanation: Right. An empty list has no first item, so line 2 raises an error. Dry-running an edge case like this, before running the code, is how you catch it.
No. The function never reaches return; line 2 fails first.
